title: Pushing a cart
prompt: A 2.0 kg cart starts at rest on a frictionless track. You push it with a constant 10 N horizontal force for 3.0 m.

steps.prompt: Which principle links your push to the cart's final speed, using the force and the distance but not the time?
options: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)
Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals change in momentum)
steps.answer: Work-energy theorem (net work equals change in kinetic energy)

feedback.Conservation of mechanical energy: Mechanical energy isn't conserved here: your push does work on the cart and adds energy.
feedback.Conservation of momentum: Momentum isn't conserved here: your push is an outside force.
feedback.Impulse-momentum theorem (impulse equals: Impulse needs how long the push lasts, and you know the distance, not the time.

steps.hint: You know a force and a distance. Force times distance is work, and the net work on the cart changes its kinetic energy.

steps.prompt: How much work, in joules, does your push do on the cart?
steps.hint: The force points along the motion, so W = Fd = 10 × 3.0.

steps.prompt: What is the cart's final speed, in m/s?
steps.hint: All 30 J becomes kinetic energy: ½(2.0)v² = 30, so v = √30.
